questions.q: Name the three revolutions identified in the NCERT text as creating the context for sociology's emergence, and state the century in which sociology was born.
questions.a: The three revolutions are: (1) The Enlightenment (or scientific revolution), (2) The French Revolution, and (3) The Industrial Revolution. Sociology was born in 19th century Western Europe. A wrong answer (e.g., naming the American Revolution or Russian Revolution, or saying 18th century) reveals the student has not distinguished the specific European processes the textbook identifies from other historical events, indicating superficial reading rather than comprehension of the causal argument.

questions.q: The NCERT states: "For reason to become the defining feature of the human world, it was necessary to displace nature, religion and the divine acts of gods from the central position they had in earlier ways of understanding the world." Explain in your own words what this displacement meant for how society came to be studied.
questions.a: This displacement meant society ceased to be seen as a divine/natural order and became a human-made construct amenable to rational analysis — making it possible to study society scientifically rather than theologically. A wrong answer (e.g., "it meant people stopped believing in God" or "science replaced religion entirely") reveals the conflation of secularisation with atheism, missing the epistemological shift: the Enlightenment didn't eliminate religion but relocated it to the private sphere, allowing society to become an object of empirical investigation — a distinction crucial for Durkheim's later concept of social facts.

questions.q: A student argues: "The French Revolution's Declaration of Human Rights only mattered for France. It didn't create conditions for sociology globally." Using the NCERT text, evaluate this claim by identifying two ways the Revolution's ideas became transnational forces shaping modern society worldwide.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. Two transnational forces: (1) The nation-state model with centralised government and sovereign citizenship became the global template, spreading through colonialism and imitation — sociology studies this universal form. (2) The public/private sphere distinction (religion/family → private; education/law → public) restructured social life everywhere modern institutions went. A wrong answer focusing only on French domestic changes misses the NCERT's explicit statement: "These processes completely transformed not only European society, but also the rest of the world as it came into contact with Europe" — revealing inability to trace global diffusion of revolutionary categories.

questions.q: Compare how the Industrial Revolution transformed the SPATIAL organisation of society (where people live) versus the TEMPORAL organisation (how time is structured). Give one concrete example of each from the NCERT text.
questions.a: Spatial: Rural→urban migration; "Cities and towns became the dominant forms of human settlement, housing large and unequal populations in small, densely populated urban areas." Temporal: Factory discipline imposed clock-time; "workers... had to work long hours in hazardous circumstances" regulated by machine rhythms not seasonal cycles. A wrong answer giving only spatial changes (or only temporal) reveals failure to recognise that industrial capitalism restructured BOTH dimensions simultaneously — a duality Marx later theorises as space-time compression, and which Weber sees in bureaucratic rationalisation.

questions.q: The NCERT states: "Modern forms of governance, with the state assuming control of health, sanitation, crime control and general 'development' created the demand for new kinds of knowledge. The social sciences and particularly sociology emerged partly as a response to this need." Critique the view that sociology was merely a tool of state control. Provide one argument supporting and one challenging this view, using text evidence.
questions.a: Supporting: The state needed "scientific information generated by the state to monitor and maintain the health of its social body" — sociology provided population statistics, deviance categories, administrative categories. Challenging: Sociology also emerged from critical thought (Marx) seeking to overthrow the capitalist order the state upheld; Durkheim sought moral reconstruction not just administration. A one-sided answer reveals inability to hold the dual character of sociology: both a science of the state AND a critique of social order — a tension central to the discipline's identity.

questions.q: Construct a 3-sentence "origin story" for sociology that a Class 11 student could tell a Class 9 student, incorporating: (a) the Enlightenment's intellectual shift, (b) the French Revolution's political subject, and (c) the Industrial Revolution's social problem. Each sentence must begin with "Because..." and end with "...sociology became necessary."
questions.a: Because the Enlightenment displaced divine authority with human reason, making society a human-made object that could be rationally analysed... sociology became necessary. Because the French Revolution created the sovereign individual and the nation-state as new political subjects requiring systematic understanding... sociology became necessary. Because the Industrial Revolution produced factory cities, wage labour, and state administration of populations that traditional knowledge could not explain or manage... sociology became necessary. A poor answer (e.g., listing events without causal links, or omitting one revolution) reveals the student cannot synthesise the three processes into a coherent explanatory narrative — the core skill for board exam long-answer questions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ (late 17th–18th century), French Revolution (1789), and Industrial Revolution (late 18th–early 19th century) constitute the three foundational historical processes that transformed European society from feudal, religiously-dominated, agrarian orders into modern, secular, industrial nation-states, thereby creating the intellectual and material conditions that necessitated the emergence of sociology as a scientific discipline to study the resulting new social realities.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you wake up in a village in 1750 ______: your life is governed by the church calendar, your labour belongs to the seigneur, and you've never travelled more than 10 km from home.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how each revolution contributed specific intellectual or material conditions for sociology's emergence, and can trace the causal chain from historical transformation → new social problems → demand for scientific knowledge of society → birth of sociology, using precise terminology (secular, sovereign individual.
